title: Saudi Arabia issues danger alerts at Yanbu, its Red Sea oil outlet, as Houthi attacks go on
dek: Yanbu is where Saudi crude has been loaded since Iran shut the Strait of Hormuz. The Saudi-led coalition also said it destroyed a Houthi missile fired towards Medina.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Saudi Arabia on Thursday issued alerts warning of potential danger in Yanbu, the Red Sea port that has become the kingdom's main outlet for oil exports since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, Reuters reported. The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said it had destroyed a missile launched by the group towards the holy city of Medina.

Saudi civil defence also sent emergency alerts to the south-eastern area of Sharurah, on the border with Yemen, according to Reuters. The alerts did not say what the threat to Yanbu was, and there were no reports of damage there by early Friday India time.

## What each side has said

The Houthis, who are aligned with Iran, had not claimed any attack on the kingdom on Thursday, Reuters reported. On Wednesday they said they had attacked Riyadh's international airport while Syria's President Ahmed al-Sharaa was visiting the kingdom. Saudi authorities have not confirmed that attack. During al-Sharaa's visit, he and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman witnessed the signing of a defence agreement; no details were released.

Saudi Arabia has in the past accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca and Medina, accusations the group has rejected, The Hindu reported.

## Background

Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed this year after the UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022 broke down. The Houthis imposed what they called a maritime embargo on the kingdom in July, and in October a missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Saudi authorities said 12 people were killed and 309 wounded in that strike, Al Jazeera reported; the Houthis claimed it and hit the airport again the next day. Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have since launched an offensive in Yemen.

The war has become another front in the wider conflict between Iran and the US and Israel. Saudi Arabia has asked countries from the US to Europe and West Asia for help. Egypt has approved military assistance, Turkey is set to ratify a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, and Britain said in October it would fly fighter jets on defensive missions over Saudi cities, according to Reuters.

## Why Yanbu matters

Since Iran shut Hormuz early this year, Saudi Arabia has pumped crude across the country through its East-West pipeline to Yanbu, so it can be loaded on the Red Sea coast instead of in the Gulf. By late March the pipeline was running at about 7 million barrels a day, Fortune reported. In September a drone attack launched from Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to close the pipeline for several days, CNBC reported, and Brent crude briefly rose to nearly $110 a barrel.

Tankers leaving Yanbu for Asia still have to pass through the Bab al-Mandab strait off Yemen, within range of the Houthis. A threat to Yanbu therefore puts at risk the main route by which Saudi oil has continued to reach buyers in Asia, including India, which imports most of the crude it uses. Saudi Arabia is one of India's largest suppliers.

For India, the risk is higher prices and longer delays at a time when oil has only just eased. Brent fell to a two-month low this week after the US midterm elections, and Indian markets rallied on the drop.

## What happens next

Saudi authorities have not said how long the alerts for Yanbu will stay in place. Iran's foreign minister has said talks with Saudi Arabia are continuing, and Riyadh has said they are meant to prevent further escalation, The Hindu reported.
